a: The first time we came home blowing into used condoms
g: OPENING — the whole engine, in one sentence
n:
**The obscenity the narrator cannot see.** The reader decodes it instantly; Musa never does, not in the whole story. Everything that follows runs on this gap. Note the detail is *technical* and admiring — endlessly stretchy, transparent — which is exactly how a ten-year-old would assess a balloon. He is not being coy. He genuinely does not know.

Compare Chantal's opening, which announces a theme. This announces a **contract**: you will understand more than the boy telling you.

a: declared my six-year-old sister Amoo
g: CRAFT — the corroborating child
n: Amoo exists to confirm the innocence is real and not a narrator's pose. A second child says the same thing, so the reader cannot suspect Musa of coyness.

a: Stay away from this Fatima
g: PLANT — the unexplained refusal
n: **No reason given, and none will be given.** Cleland's gap: the reader supplies the reason immediately, the narrator never does. The mother is characterised here as arbitrary — which is the misreading the story wants for the next 25%.

a: knocking me onto the ground with her forearm
g: TURN − · the mother reads as antagonist
n: Violence, unexplained. **File this — it re-reads completely after the illiteracy line.** Right now she is a woman who hits her son over balloons. Later she is a woman with no other instrument.

a: while hammering on the gate with her clenched fist
g: PLANT — she has the name wrong
n:
**Faridah, not Fatima.** Musa whispers the correction; she ignores it and carries on shouting the wrong name in a stranger's compound. 

This is the first evidence of what the story is about and it is disguised as temper. She cannot hold the name. Placed ~60 lines before the reveal.

a: beholding a mad woman and her ten-year-old son
g: CRAFT — the one exterior view
n: The only sentence where Musa sees his own mother from outside, through neighbours' eyes. **He never does it again.** Shame rendered as a change of camera position, not as a feeling.

a: Always something in there for you to learn
g: PLANT — the father owns literacy
n: Father = newspapers, crosswords, vocabulary, ten articles. **The mother will turn out to own none of it.** The contrast is built here and never remarked on.

a: Which class are you, again
g: CRAFT — characterisation by question
n: Three words establish an absent father more efficiently than a paragraph could. He does not know what class his son is in. **McKee: reveal character through choice under pressure — including the choice not to have noticed.**

a: but I needed some money
g: COMPETENCE — Y
n: **The story's competence test, passed here.** Musa is an expert at one thing: extracting money as a child with none. Inventing a torn shoe. This recurs — pricing utensils against a football, trading a Jabulani for boots. Gardner's rule that a protagonist must be *good at something* the reader isn't.

a: they had run out of stock
g: TURN − · the reader winces, the child concludes
n: **He has been to every shop on the street asking for condoms.** He reports the outcome as market research. The comedy and the horror are the same sentence — which is the register the whole story is written in, and the register neither Chantal nor Beat of My Hurt has anywhere.

a: they your savings
g: CRAFT — Fatima made human in one line
n: She laughs at him. Not seductive, not sinister — amused by a child. **The story refuses to make her either a victim or a predator**, which is why the ending hurts.

a: This money, who gave it to you
g: BEAT — the escalation engine
n: Second discovery, second march to the gate. Barrett's economy: the same action twice, raised. The third time it happens it will be at a football pitch in front of a crowd.

a: rather be a polytechnic whore than an illiterate jobless saint
g: THE TURN — the hinge of the entire story
n:
**Everything before this line re-reads at once.** The wrong name at the gate. The forearm. The refusal to explain. The delegated homework. 

Rubric axis 5, *the gap so wide it reorganises the reader's understanding* — this is a 5, and it is delivered by a **minor character in dialogue**, not by the narrator, who does not understand it yet.

Note it is not the narrator's discovery. It is the reader's. Musa gets there two scenes later.

a: A silence fell over the compound
g: CRAFT — the audience is the wound
n: *The other tenants were witnessing.* The injury is not the word, it is the witnesses. Same mechanism at the climax.

a: The sandal from her right foot was missing
g: WITHHOLDING — the fight happens offstage
n: **The physical fight is not shown.** A missing sandal and a muddied lesu carry the whole of it. The story consistently refuses its own dramatic scenes and reports the residue instead.

a: suddenly asked at dinner
g: BEAT — the six-year-old asks the unaskable
n: The question is given to Amoo, not Musa. **The narrator is spared having to be cruel**, and the story gets its scene anyway. A structural dodge, and a good one.

a: responded Mother, three forks later
g: CRAFT — the delay is the answer
n: **Three forks.** The denial is worthless and the measurement of the pause is what tells you. Cleland's sentence-level suspense: the timing carries what the words deny.

a: something had shrunk inside of Mother
g: MOTIF — the only interiority she is ever given
n: The one time Musa attributes an inner state to his mother in 5,000 words — **and he does not name it.** *I didn't know what, but something had shrunk.* Rubric axis 3 at its highest setting: the reader knows what the narrator won't say, because the narrator genuinely cannot say it.

a: And then it started falling into place, everything
g: PAYOFF — the retroactive re-read, stated once
n: The narrator catches up with the reader. **Once, in one sentence, and then he moves on.** Compare the temptation to spend a paragraph here. Homework always delegated to Halima; never heard her speak English at parent evenings. Two pieces of evidence, no commentary.

a: never heard Mother speaking English
g: PLANT paid — parent-teacher meetings
n: The detail that hurts most, because it means she went, and sat there, and said nothing.

a: Two hissing tyres and a buried knife later
g: LEAKAGE + character
n: The tyre-puncturing is the mother's only lever over her husband and it requires her son's hands. Funny, sad, and it produces the job. **Cut it and the plot survives — but she never becomes a person.**

a: Who taught you the ways of a merchant
g: CRAFT — the character in six words
n: Her exasperation is also accurate. The story's best joke about its own protagonist.

a: she had got herself a job
g: TURN + · the only upward move in the story
n: And the narrator claims credit for it. *I felt good about it, that I had been of immense utility.* **He is wrong about why it happened and right that he caused it** — the exact ratio of understanding this narrator is allowed.

a: we could retire our mothers immediately
g: CRAFT — the dream is filial
n: The football fantasy is not about glory, it is about the mother. Planted here, so that the climax — the mother destroying the football — is a collision of the same wish with itself.

a: My overbite was noticeable to everybody but my parents
g: LEAKAGE — pure surplus
n: Serves nothing. Never returns. **This is the x-factor**: a private vanity with no plot function, which is how the reader knows there is a whole boy here and not a device.

a: The greedy school administration had leased the football field to a driving school
g: LEAKAGE — a whole subplot the plot does not need
n: Runs for a page and a half. Encroachment, negotiation, free car washes, traffic cones for goalposts, an audience of adults. **The world was here before the story and continues after it.** Nazir scored 5 on this axis for exactly this kind of material.

a: hey, why not share the field
g: CRAFT — comedy as the delivery of powerlessness
n: The children win the negotiation by washing the cars of the people who took their field. **The joke is the analysis.**

a: the pale yellowish-white of his fragmented femur
g: LEAKAGE — the darkest image in the story serves no plot
n: Pinto is run over, never comes back, and the field is banned. **He is not a metaphor and he is not foreshadowing.** A life crosses the frame and leaves. This is the single hardest thing to imitate and the clearest marker of a world-class story.

a: recited it like it was the Lord
g: THE CONTROLLING IDEA, dramatised, never stated
n:
**Fatima can spell.** That is the whole reason Musa is in her house and he never once says so. The mother cannot help with homework; the neighbour answers instantly. 

Rubric axis 7 — *never stated, impossible to miss.* The story's title is about a mother you cannot find; its subject is a boy who found a substitute.

a: He presented me with a pair three sizes too big
g: LEAKAGE — the cobbler
n: Unkempt white beard, greets him like an agemate, knows Jabulanis. Two scenes, no plot function beyond shoes, and he is completely alive.

a: your sister or mother
g: PLANT — the substitution named by someone else
n: Nabongho asks the question the story will not ask. **Sister or mother.** Musa does not answer it on the page.

a: waited like I had when it was Dan
g: THE LIST — the story's most-copied move
n:
**A ten-year-old keeping an accurate register of the men.** He reports it as a household rule about shoes and porches. The reader assembles what Fatima does for a living from a child's list of names.

Nothing is stated. Nothing needs to be.

a: told me to wait when it was Sumaiyah
g: THE CLAUSE THAT PROVES HE COUNTS
n:
**The exception.** One woman, and he was not asked to wait. 

This single clause converts the list from a coincidence into a *tally* — it proves he has been noticing the pattern for a long time, and it does so without him ever knowing what the pattern means. Six words. There is nothing better than this in either of your drafts.

a: tell her to reconsider
g: TURN − · coercion routed through a child
n:
**Coach uses Musa as the courier for a threat.** The reader understands the whole arrangement — the sideline conversations, the forgotten officiating, the selection. Musa: *Reconsider what?*

And he delivers it. He passes the message on to Fatima verbatim, proud to be useful.

a: why are you always bothering me
g: MISREAD — the reader and the narrator split furthest here
n: Musa reads this as rejection. The reader reads a cornered woman refusing to sign a child out of school for a man who has been pressuring her. **The gap between the two readings is the widest in the story.**

a: Fatima was nothing but a selfish polytechnic whore
g: TURN − · the child adopts the mother's word
n:
He does not know what *polytechnic* means. He does not know what the other word means either. **He has learned the sentence and uses it as a weapon on the one adult who taught him anything.** 

The story's cruellest line and the narrator does not feel it.

a: Her head was bowed, she must
g: PLANT — she is not watching
n: He scores a penalty and looks for her; she is on her phone. Planted so the climax can find her still oblivious, still sitting there, when the mother reaches her.

a: gesticulating furiously at him
g: CLIMAX — the third march, in public, at ~87%
n:
**The escalation completes.** The compound, the compound again, now a stadium. Same action three times, each with a larger audience. Barrett's structure, exactly.

Note the climax is not a discovery. Everyone already knows everything. **It is a humiliation, staged.**

a: What do you mean does he know me
g: THE LINE
n: *He's my son!* — a woman shouting proof of a relationship because she has no other document of it. The title is in this sentence.

a: her toes dancing in a show of restraint
g: CRAFT — the object carries it
n:
**Bare feet on the grass.** She lost or abandoned her shoes getting there. He is looking at the ground because he cannot look at her face, and what is on the ground is the whole distance she travelled. 

Writing Constitution: *objects carry emotion.* This is how.

a: Mother was misty-eyed, lips quivering
g: BEAT — the first crying in the story
n: After the forearm, the screaming, the compound. She cries only when she has to ask her son a question in front of a crowd.

a: I looked Mother straight in the face, for the first time
g: TURN + and − simultaneously — the one active choice
n:
**The protagonist acts, once, in the whole story, and it destroys the person he loves.** *I came with Fatima.*

Rubric axis 4 at its highest: the turn is not the expected one. He does not defy his mother and he does not lie. He looks at her — for the first time in the story, which is the reveal — and gives Fatima up.

a: I ran the whole way home, cold wind inflaming my eyes
g: CRAFT — the refused word
n: **He will not say crying.** He attributes it to the wind. Cleland's banned telling-words, obeyed at the exact moment it costs most.

a: emptied of everything but her scent
g: MOTIF — polytechnic
n: *That redolent polytechnic scent.* He has attached his mother's insult to a smell he loves. The word has become his, permanently, and he still does not know what it means.

a: that I was hoping to marry her someday
g: THE GUT PUNCH — what the relationship actually was
n: **Withheld until she is gone.** A ten-year-old's understanding of the thing the reader has been watching, delivered flat, in a subordinate clause, after the door is open and the house is empty.

a: have spoken Luganda
g: CRAFT — a joke immediately before the ending
n: Fake Ronaldo, exposed by his Luganda. **The story earns its last blow by making you laugh eight words before it.**

a: a thousand Fatimas, most of them white, none of them polytechnic
g: RESONANT CLOSE — the title detonates
n:
**Mothers Not Appearing in Search.** The search fails; the title was the ending all along; and it does not say *mother*, it says *Fatima* — so the reader has to make the substitution the story has refused to state for 5,000 words.

*None of them polytechnic* — he still has the word and still does not have the meaning. **The narrator ends exactly as ignorant as he began, and the reader ends knowing everything.** That is the form completing itself.
